summary: Computer vision syndrome (CVS) is a condition caused by prolonged, uninterrupted focusing on a computer or other display, leaving eye muscles unable to recover from sustained tension. The note lists its symptoms, aggravating factors such as poor lighting and air flow, and therapies including rest, breaks, the 20-20-20 rule, artificial tears, humidifiers, dark interfaces, supplements, and eyeglasses. It also reviews evidence on blue-light lenses and reports prevalence figures from a US NIOSH statement and a Malaysian student study.
one_line: Overview of computer vision syndrome, a strain condition from prolonged screen use, with its symptoms, therapies, eyeglass evidence and prevalence.
key_facts: Computer vision syndrome (CVS) results from focusing the eyes on a computer or other display device for protracted, uninterrupted periods of time.
Symptoms of CVS include headaches, blurred vision, neck pain, fatigue, eye strain, dry eyes, irritated eyes, double vision, vertigo/dizziness, polyopia, and difficulty refocusing the eyes.
Glare, strong blue-spectrum backlights, bright overhead lighting, and air moving past the eyes can aggravate CVS symptoms.
The '20–20–20 rule' recommends that every 20 minutes, the eyes focus on an object 20 feet (6 meters) away for 20 seconds.

A 2017 randomized controlled trial of macular carotenoid supplements (lutein, zeaxanthin, and mesozeaxanthin) found significant reductions in self-reported headache, eye strain, eye fatigue and sleep complaints in people with high screen time.
A 2021 review found little supporting evidence for bi- or multi-focal glasses or blue-light-blocking glasses for CVS, and reported 'low-certainty' support for omega-3 supplements.
Decreased focusing capability is mitigated by wearing a small plus-powered (+1.00 to +1.50) over-the-counter pair of eyeglasses.

A Pacific University study of 36 participants found amber colored lenses improved eye irritation, tearing, dry eyes and tired eyes versus placebo lenses, but the same team could not reproduce the results in a 2008 follow-up study.
A lens-industry-sponsored study reported theoretical reductions in phototoxicity of 10.6% to 23.6% from blue light-filtering lenses, and over 70% of participants were unable to detect these changes.
Double-blind trials have shown no evidence supporting blue light filtering lenses for digital eye strain caused by blue light from electronic screens.
According to the US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, computer vision syndrome affects about 90% of people who spend three hours or more a day at a computer.
A Malaysian study of 795 university students aged 18 to 25 found that 89.9% of those surveyed experienced some type of CVS symptom.
Observations from persons with chronic eye strain suggest most people who claim to get enough sleep are not, and seven to eight hours of uninterrupted sleep allows eye muscles to recover.
